#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures. Replace these with your original study's
# values, and say in a comment exactly where in the paper each one comes from.
#
# Rios et al., (2024), Experiment 3 lists N = 105: Used the data file provided in the osf project 
# to determine how many participants were in each condition. Found that 52 participants were in the
# manipulation condition and 53 participants were in the control.
#
# Means, SDs and 95% CIs by condition: Table 4 (p. 4), Experiment 3 columns.
# F tests and partial eta squared: Results, p. 4 ("In the last of the three experiments ...").
# "Intervention" is the paper's Jewish identity salient condition.
original <- tribble(
  ~outcome,     ~condition,     ~n, ~mean, ~sd,   ~ci_low, ~ci_high,
  "diversity",  "Intervention", 52,  4.38,  1.18,   4.06,    4.70,
  "diversity",  "Control",      53,  3.91,  1.14,   3.60,    4.23,
  "white_priv", "Intervention", 52,  5.65,  1.55,   5.21,    6.09,
  "white_priv", "Control",      53,  5.41,  1.66,   4.97,    5.85,
  "bias",       "Intervention", 52, -7.66, 21.21, -14.39,   -0.94,
  "bias",       "Control",      53, -6.80, 27.26, -13.47,   -0.14
)
original_tests <- tribble(
  ~outcome,     ~F,    ~df2, ~p,    ~eta2p,
  "diversity",  4.25,  103,  0.042, 0.040,
  "white_priv", 0.561, 103,  0.455, 0.005,
  "bias",       0.032, 103,  0.858, 0.0003
)

# The key outcome (perceived personal contributions to diversity) and readable outcome names.
key_outcome <- "diversity"
outcome_labels <- c(diversity  = "Perceived personal contributions to diversity",
                    white_priv = "White privilege awareness",
                    bias       = "Intergroup bias (White − minorities)")

# Key statistics

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Score the scales. All Likert items are 1-7. Reverse-worded items are reversed (8 - x)
# before averaging: WhitePriv_4 ("I do not feel that White people have any benefits ..."),
# and items 1, 3 and 8 of both identification scales ("... has very little to do with how I
# feel about myself", "... is unimportant to ...", "... is NOT a major factor ..."). The
# paper does not list its reverse-scored items; these were checked against the papers the
# scales come from (Swim & Miller, 1999; Sellers et al., 1997).
score_scales <- function(d) {
  reversed <- c("WhitePriv_4", "JewishID_1", "JewishID_3", "JewishID_8",
                "WhiteID_1", "WhiteID_3", "WhiteID_8")
  item_mean <- function(cols) {
    m <- rowMeans(cols, na.rm = TRUE)
    ifelse(is.nan(m), NA, m)
  }
  d |>
    mutate(across(all_of(reversed), ~ 8 - .x)) |>
    mutate(
      diversity       = item_mean(pick(DivFeelings_1:DivFeelings_5)),
      # Thermometers: 1 = White Americans; 2-6 = Black, Hispanic/Latino, Asian, Middle
      # Eastern and Native Americans; 7-10 = gay men, lesbian women, transgender and
      # bisexual individuals. Bias is White minus the minority average (p. 7), so higher
      # scores mean more favourable evaluations of White Americans.
      white_warmth    = FeelingThermo_1,
      minority_warmth = item_mean(pick(FeelingThermo_2:FeelingThermo_6)),
      bias            = white_warmth - minority_warmth,
      lgbt            = item_mean(pick(FeelingThermo_7:FeelingThermo_10)),
      white_priv      = item_mean(pick(WhitePriv_1:WhitePriv_5)),
      jewish_id       = item_mean(pick(JewishID_1:JewishID_8)),
      white_id        = item_mean(pick(WhiteID_1:WhiteID_8))
    )
}

# Load one phase's de-identified data, apply the exclusion rule, and score the scales. Returns
# NULL if that phase's file does not exist yet, which is how every section below knows to
# skip itself. `steps` keeps everyone remaining after each exclusion, for the funnel table.
read_phase <- function(file) {
  if (!file.exists(file)) return(NULL)
  # `condition` is the assigned condition, from the Condition embedded data field that the
  # Qualtrics randomizer sets (labelled in deidentify-data.qmd).
  started <- read.csv(file) |> mutate(assigned = condition)

  # Exclusion rule (Analysis plan), applied in this order: did not finish, religion not Jewish
  # (Religion == 4), failed the attention check (AttentionCheck == 3 is "Yellow"), in the
  # intervention condition did not say they belong to a minority group (IdentitySalient == 1
  # is "Yes"), and outliers on the key measure. Files de-identified before Finished was kept
  # skip the first step.
  complete <- if ("Finished" %in% names(started)) {
    filter(started, Finished %in% c(1, "1", TRUE, "TRUE", "True"))
  } else started
  jewish   <- filter(complete, Religion %in% 4)
  attended <- filter(jewish, AttentionCheck %in% 3)
  minority <- filter(attended, assigned == "Control" | IdentitySalient %in% 1) |> score_scales()

  # Outliers, as in the original (p. 9): Cook's D for the ANOVA of condition on perceived
  # personal contributions to diversity, excluding anyone whose D is more than 3 SD above the
  # sample mean of D. Participants with no diversity score have no D and are not excluded here.
  minority$cooks_d <- NA_real_
  scored <- !is.na(minority$diversity) & !is.na(minority$assigned)
  if (sum(scored) > 2 && n_distinct(minority$assigned[scored]) == 2) {
    minority$cooks_d[scored] <- cooks.distance(lm(diversity ~ assigned, data = minority[scored, ]))
  }
  d_cutoff <- mean(minority$cooks_d, na.rm = TRUE) + 3 * sd(minority$cooks_d, na.rm = TRUE)
  keep <- filter(minority, is.na(cooks_d) | is.na(d_cutoff) | cooks_d <= d_cutoff)

  list(started = started, keep = keep, cooks_d_cutoff = d_cutoff,
       steps = list(`Started` = started, `Finished the study` = complete,
                    `Religion is Jewish` = jewish, `Passed the attention check` = attended,
                    `Intervention: said they belong to a minority group` = minority,
                    `Not an outlier (Cook's D)` = keep))
}

# Per-condition summary of one outcome: n, mean, SD and 95% CI. The original study enters
# the analysis in this same form (from Table 4), so both go through identical code below.
condition_summary <- function(d, outcome = key_outcome) {
  d$keep |>
    filter(!is.na(.data[[outcome]])) |>
    group_by(condition = assigned) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(.data[[outcome]]), sd = sd(.data[[outcome]]),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(se = sd / sqrt(n),
           ci_low  = mean - qt(0.975, n - 1) * se,
           ci_high = mean + qt(0.975, n - 1) * se) |>
    select(-se)
}

# The key statistic: the one-way ANOVA of condition (two groups), computed from the
# per-condition summary. With two groups F = t^2 from the pooled-variance t test, and
# partial eta squared = F / (F + df). The estimate is intervention minus control.
diff_ci <- function(s) {
  tr <- s[s$condition == "Intervention", ]
  ct <- s[s$condition == "Control", ]
  if (nrow(tr) == 0 || nrow(ct) == 0 || tr$n < 2 || ct$n < 2) return(NULL)
  df2 <- tr$n + ct$n - 2
  sd_pooled <- sqrt(((tr$n - 1) * tr$sd^2 + (ct$n - 1) * ct$sd^2) / df2)
  se <- sd_pooled * sqrt(1 / tr$n + 1 / ct$n)
  est <- tr$mean - ct$mean
  t <- est / se
  tibble(N = tr$n + ct$n, estimate = est,
         ci_low = est - qt(0.975, df2) * se, ci_high = est + qt(0.975, df2) * se,
         d = est / sd_pooled, F = t^2, df2 = df2, p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df2),
         eta2p = t^2 / (t^2 + df2))
}

# Side-by-side figure: condition means with 95% CIs for any number of studies, on the same
# axes and in the order given. Each study is a condition_summary()-style tibble.
comparison_plot <- function(..., outcome = key_outcome) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Control", "Intervention"),
                              labels = c("Control", "Identity salient")),
           label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  colours <- setNames(c("grey45", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.5)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = mean, colour = Study)) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), position = dodge, size = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(y = ci_low, label = label), position = dodge, vjust = 1.6, size = 3,
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = if (outcome %in% c("diversity", "white_priv")) c(1, 7),
                       breaks = if (outcome %in% c("diversity", "white_priv")) 1:7 else waiver()) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = colours) +
    labs(x = "Condition", y = outcome_labels[[outcome]], colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(phase1_file)
phase2 <- read_phase(phase2_file)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)

original_key <- filter(original, outcome == key_outcome)
```


```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_p <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< .001" else sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p))
fmt_row <- function(study, r, collected = TRUE) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    status <- if (collected) "not enough data (needs 2+ analysed per condition)" else "not yet collected"
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Difference (salient − control)` = status,
                  `95% CI` = "", F = "", p = "", `η²p` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Difference (salient − control)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         F = sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f", r$df2, r$F),
         p = fmt_p(r$p), `η²p` = sprintf("%.3f", r$eta2p))
}
# The original's difference and CI are recomputed from Table 4; its F, p and eta squared are
# the values the paper reports (recomputing them from rounded means gives F = 4.31).
orig_reported <- diff_ci(original_key) |>
  mutate(select(filter(original_tests, outcome == key_outcome), F, df2, p, eta2p))
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", orig_reported),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) diff_ci(condition_summary(phase1)), have_data),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) diff_ci(condition_summary(phase2)), have_phase2)
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllrr",
               caption = "Key comparison: perceived personal contributions to diversity (1–7), identity salient minus control, with a one-way ANOVA of condition.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

I am interested in the ethnic-racial identity development of Latine youth, what factors can promote or hinder ethnic-racial identity development, and whether ethnic-racial identity can be used to increase solidarity across groups. I was interested in Rios et al. (2024) because it is an experiment that manipulated ethnic-racial identity salience by asking participants if they belonged to an ethnic-racial minority group (including religious groups) to see if it would decrease intergroup bias, increase personal feelings of diversity, and increase White privilege awareness. This study included participants that were Jewish and identified racially as White. The original study found that invoking ethnic-racial identity among Jewish participants did decrease intergroup bias across three experiments and increased personal feelings of diversity in the thrid experiment. I plan to replicate only the final experiment, Experiment 3, because it is the only experiment of the three that analyzed data with the smallest sample.

For this study, I created a survey with two conditions, one that invoked ethnic-racial identity and one that does not mention it. I preregistered one-way ANOVA testing for the effect of condition on feelings about diversity. A potential extension of the study I could undertake would be to add a condition that could invoke feelings of belonging to the ethnic-racial majority group (i.e., White).


## Methods

### Power analysis

The original effect size was given in the paper as η2p = 0.04, which can be interpretted as being between a small and medium effect. Based on the table below, 192 participants would be needed if I wanted to use 80% power as the paper did. Another possibility is to collect 2.5 times the original sample (263 participants). While each option would be ideal to see if the effect still holds, both are not feasible due to a small amount of Jewish American participants being active on Prolific (395 in the past 90 days). As a result, I set the sample to be the same as the original study instead.


```{r}
#| label: power
# Effect size from the original's reported partial eta squared, converted to Cohen's f.
# power.anova.test() takes the variance of the group means (between.var, computed with
# n - 1) relative to the within-group variance, and returns n PER GROUP. With two groups
# and within.var = 1, between.var = 2 * f^2.
original_eta2p <- original_tests$eta2p[original_tests$outcome == key_outcome]
original_f <- sqrt(original_eta2p / (1 - original_eta2p))

power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- ceiling(power.anova.test(groups = 2, between.var = 2 * original_f^2, within.var = 1,
                                sig.level = 0.05, power = pw)$n)
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = n, n_total = 2 * n)
})

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * sum(original_key$n))

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per condition", "N total"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original effect (η²p = %.3f, f = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .05.",
               original_eta2p, original_f))
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half`.

### Planned sample

The planned sample size was the same as the original study's sample size (N = 105) due to the small participant pool of Jewish Americans on Prolific that the original study had encountered. This small participant pool persists today with about 395 potential participants being eligible at the time of the study launch. The sample frame was US residents on Prolific who listed a religious affiliation to Jewish and listed their race/ethnicity as White/Sephardic Jew or White/Caucasian. They will also be 18 years or older and fluent in English. The specific eligibility criteria were selected on Prolific so that a screening survey was not necessary. Recruitment will continue until 105 participants pass the exclusion criteria below.

### Materials

The exact materials were obtained from the osf link provided in the article (https://osf.io/gh3nx). The file containing the materials ("Jewish_identity_Prolific_April_2023.docx") can be found under the associated project link (https://osf.io/rmx7f).

### Procedure

At the beginning of the study, participants see the consent text provided in the Class Prolific Guidelines page on Canvas. Then, "[p]articipants were randomly assigned to either the Jewish identity salient condition or control condition and completed the experimental manipulation, followed by the measure of perceived personal contributions to diversity from the correlational study (M = 4.14, SD = 1.18; α = 0.82) and the feeling thermometer items from Experiment 2 (evaluations of White Americans: M = 66.93, SD = 24.16; average evaluation of racial/ethnic minorities: M = 74.16, SD = 19.45, α = 0.94; intergroup bias composite: M = -7.23, SD = 24.34; LGBT composite: M = 70.62, SD = 24.13, α = 0.93). Next, participants completed the measures of White privilege awareness (M = 5.53, SD = 1.60; α = 0.96), Jewish identification (M = 5.24, SD = 1.19; α = 0.91), and White identification (M = 3.26, SD = 1.29; α = 0.89) from the correlational study" (Rios et al., 2024)

Afterwards, participants were asked to write in their Prolific ID number and fill out several demographic questions pertaining to their age, residence in the United States, religious affiliation and practices, race/ethnicity, gender, political affiliation, and education level. Once the demographic questions were complete. They reach the end of the study where they are thanked for their time and are debriefed on the study's purpose.

From start to finish, the study should take between 5 - 10 minutes.

### Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** As part of the analysis, I composed a 5-item composite score for personal feelings of diversity. Then, I used a one-way ANOVA test for the effect of condition on this 5-item composite score on personal feelings of diversity. This is the same test used in the original paper that found an effect based on condition.

Additionally, I also used a one-way ANOVA test for the effect of condition on intergroup bias. This was computed by taking the average feelings of warmth for all ethnic/racial minority groups listed in the feelings thermomenter and taking the difference between it and feelings of warmth towards White/European Americans.

Lastly, another one-way ANOVA test was conducted for the effect of condition on White privilege awareness (another 5-item composite).

**Exclusions.** Participants are excluded if they did not complete the study, if they did not select that they are part of an ethnic/racial or religious minority group in the Jewish salience condition, if they did not select their religious affiliation as Jewish, if they failed the attention check, or if they are a statistical outlier. If a participant's Cook's D score is greater than 3 SD from the sample mean, they will be considered a statistical outlier and excluded.

## Results

### Data preparation
Due to using Qualtrics for data collection, I needed to download my data manually and deidentify it before I could begin working with it. To deidentify the data, I created a separate file titled "deidentify-data.qmd" and wrote the code with the help of Claude. Once the data was deidentified and new participant IDs were assigned, I was able to use it in this report. 

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
rep_key <- condition_summary(phase1)

if (!is.null(diff_ci(rep_key))) {
  # One-way ANOVA of condition on perceived personal contributions to diversity, as in the
  # original. Its F and p match diff_ci(), which the tables below use.
  print(summary(aov(diversity ~ assigned, data = keep)))
} else {
  message("ANOVA not run: it needs at least two analysed participants in each condition; ",
          "there are ", nrow(keep), " in the analysis set.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: secondary
#| eval: !expr have_data
# The two further ANOVAs in the analysis plan, alongside the original's reported results.
secondary <- c("white_priv", "bias")
map_dfr(c(key_outcome, secondary), function(o) {
  r <- diff_ci(condition_summary(phase1, o))
  ot <- filter(original_tests, outcome == o)
  tibble(Outcome = outcome_labels[[o]],
         `Original` = sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f, p = %s, η²p = %.3f", ot$df2, ot$F, fmt_p(ot$p), ot$eta2p),
         `Replication` = if (is.null(r)) "not enough data" else
           sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f, p = %s, η²p = %.3f", r$df2, r$F, fmt_p(r$p), r$eta2p))
}) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "One-way ANOVAs of condition on each outcome in the analysis plan. The first row is the key analysis.")
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and
does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or
a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- diff_ci(original_key)
rep  <- diff_ci(rep_key)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (salient − control)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              `Cohen's d` = sprintf("%.2f", d),
              `η²p` = sprintf("%.3f", eta2p)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: difference in perceived personal contributions to diversity (1–7 scale), both rows computed from condition means and SDs.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants in each condition.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f scale points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Mean perceived personal contributions to diversity (1–7) by condition, original study (Rios et al., 2024, Table 4, Experiment 3) and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original_key, `Phase 1: replication` = rep_key)
```

### Exploratory analyses

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so
they generate hypotheses rather than test them.
:::

## Discussion

### Summary of replication attempt

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Open with one paragraph summarizing the result of the key analysis and your assessment of
whether the original finding replicated, partially replicated, or failed to replicate. Base
that judgment on the replication assessment above: the size of the effect relative to the
original, not just the p value.
:::

### Commentary

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Open-ended commentary, none of it long: (a) what the exploratory analyses suggest; (b) what the
replication means, for example whether the differences between your study and the original are
definitely, plausibly, or unlikely to be moderators of the result; and (c) any objections or
challenges raised by you or the original authors.
:::

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If
  your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the
  failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical
  changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design
  where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
  larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication
  succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one
  added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the
original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the
Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from
the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement,
Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or
Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same
materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the
demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare
with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a
rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new
comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you
have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
#| eval: FALSE
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants per condition in Phase 2

p1_counts <- if (have_data) risky_counts(phase1)
p1_stats  <- if (have_data) diff_ci(p1_counts)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(gain = p1_counts$risky[p1_counts$condition == "gain"] / p1_counts$n[p1_counts$condition == "gain"],
       loss = p1_counts$risky[p1_counts$condition == "loss"] / p1_counts$n[p1_counts$condition == "loss"],
       source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(gain = original_p_gain, loss = original_p_loss, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the difference at n per condition.
half_width <- function(n) 1.96 * sqrt(basis$gain * (1 - basis$gain) / n + basis$loss * (1 - basis$loss) / n)
power_at <- function(n, p1, p2) {
  tryCatch(power.prop.test(n = n, p1 = p1, p2 = p2, sig.level = 0.05)$power, error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, 2 * phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.0f points", 100 * (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.0f points (expected)", 100 * half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.0f points", 100 * (original_p_loss - original_p_gain)),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.0f points", 100 * p1_stats$estimate),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.0f points", 50 * (original_p_loss - original_p_gain))),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_p_gain, original_p_loss),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, basis$gain, basis$loss),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_p_gain, original_p_gain + (original_p_loss - original_p_gain) / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test at %d per condition, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n_per_group))
```

## Analysis plan

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

The confirmatory analysis for Phase 2, written before Phase 2 data collection. On the
best-practices tracks this is normally the same key test as Phase 1, run on the Phase 2 data
alone; say whether you will also report a pooled estimate across phases, and label it
exploratory if so. On the scientific track, specify the test for the new comparison. Name the
exclusion rule (unchanged unless it is in the Changes table) and list any exploratory measures.

Run Phase 2 under a new `EXPERIMENT.id` in `experiment.js` (for example `smith2016-phase2`) and
set `experiment_id_phase2` at the top of this file to match, so the two phases' data never mix.
:::

#| label: phase2-notice

  cat(

```{r}
#| label: phase2-results
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
p2_key   <- condition_summary(phase2)
p2_stats <- diff_ci(p2_key)
cat(sprintf("Phase 2: %d started, %d analysed.\n", nrow(phase2$started), nrow(phase2$keep)))
if (!is.null(p2_stats)) {
  cat(sprintf("Key comparison: %.2f [%.2f, %.2f], F(1, %d) = %.2f, p %s, partial eta squared = %.3f.\n",
              p2_stats$estimate, p2_stats$ci_low, p2_stats$ci_high, p2_stats$df2,
              p2_stats$F, if (p2_stats$p < 0.001) "< .001" else paste("=", fmt_p(p2_stats$p)),
              p2_stats$eta2p))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-phase2
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
#| fig-cap: "Mean perceived personal contributions to diversity (1–7) by condition: original study, Phase 1 replication, and Phase 2 extension. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

                `Phase 1: replication` = if (have_data) condition_summary(phase1),
                `Phase 2: extension` = condition_summary(phase2))
```

reasons recover the effect? For a scientific extension, what does the new condition show? End
